blocks.text: The low pressure, low resistance, high compliance capacitive sector retains approximately 75-80% of the blood volume in the venous system, right heart, pulmonary circulation, left atrium, and left ventricle in diastole. The remainder of the blood volume is in the peripheral capillaries which are part of the low pressure system.
Blood velocity increases from capillaries to large veins.
The flow speed depends on the flow rate and the cross-sectional area:
-in a tube whose diameter and therefore the cross-sectional area are constant, the speed is directly proportional to the flow rate;
-in a tube of variable diameter, the speed is inversely proportional to the sectional area for the same flow rate; the speed is greater in narrow sections than in wider sections (see diagram)
-conduction vessels: bring blood back to the heart;
-reservoir or capacitance vessels: store blood which can be mobilized when necessary.
The importance of the physiological role of this reservoir lies in its passive variations (under the effect, for example, of hydrostatic pressure) or active variations (by venoconstriction).
Wall and section of the vein
The wall of veins is thinner than arteries of the same order of division, mainly due to a thinner media.

Collagen fibers are relatively abundant. Their distensibility is therefore modest, while their mechanical resistance is high under normal conditions. This allows the vein wall to withstand very high tension.
The proportion of elastic fibers is less important than those of the arteries.
Due to its relative thinness, the venous wall is easily deformable, and the section of the vein is likely to change shape depending on the endoluminal pressure (see diagram).
Wall and section of the vein
In addition, veins are (on average twice) more numerous than arteries at the same level of division, and larger in diameter, so that the venous network is characterized by a large capacity.
Certain veins such as the splanchnic veins being richly innervated, their vasomotion allows their capacity to be modified, giving the venous sector the role of a reservoir with variable capacity.

Other veins, such as those of skeletal striated muscles, do not have such innervation, and the blood volume they contain can only be mobilized by the contraction of the muscle masses surrounding them.
The intima of certain veins has opposite semi-lunar folds, the valves, constituting a device opposing the upstream blood flow.
The valves are more numerous as the vein is small in diameter and located far from the heart, e.g. upper and lower limbs.
The pressure in the venules which collect the blood at the exit from the capillary vessels is close to 10 to 15mmHg; in a subject in a horizontal position.
Anastomoses: successive meeting of the vessels to give two main veins connected to the heart: inferior vena cava and superior vena cava.
The resistance to blood flow is low and practically zero.
The flow velocity increases from the Venules to the large veins.
The veins behave like flexible-walled tubes, they tend to collapse when the transmural pressure is negative (external pressure greater than internal pressure):
transmural pressure = intravascular (internal) pressure - extravascular (external) pressure.
When filling a collapsed vein with liquid perfused under pressure, there is an increase in volume: a low filling pressure causes a significant increase in volume.
The ratio C=ΔV/ΔPt represents the compliance of the vein.
Transmural pressure = intravascular pressure - extravascular pressure
Transmural pressure increases when intravascular pressure ˃ extravascular pressure (1)
Transmural pressure decreases when intravascular pressure ˂ extravascular pressure (2)
-When the transmural pressure increases(1), the volume increases and therefore compliance increases
-When the transmural pressure decreases(2), the volume decreases and therefore compliance decreases.
Influence of gravity on venous pressure
Moving from a lying position to a standing position causes an increase in the blood volume contained in the veins of the lower limbs.
Influence of gravity on venous pressure

The increase in volume results in an increase in venous pressure (Pv) through the effect of hydrostatic pressure (PH) on Pv: hydrostatic pressure being the pressure due to the weight of the blood inside the vessels.

blocks.text: Venomotricity is due to the presence of muscle fibers in the wall of the veins, it makes it possible to modulate the diameter and compliance of the veins, and to adjust the blood volume contained in the veins.
Contraction of the smooth muscles of the veins causes a reduction in the diameter and compliance of the veins, and an increase in venous pressure.
In the normal state, the wall of the veins does not present any active tone. Venous tone can increase under the effect of nervous or humoral stimuli:

1-sympathetic nerve stimulation: venoconstriction with reduction in venous diameter and compliance, responsible for mobilization of a significant blood volume towards the right heart, therefore resulting in an increase in venous return.
2-humoral stimulation: circulating catecholamines, angiotensin II, etc.
Venous return is the flow of blood, expressed in ml/min, which returns from the systemic veins to the right atrium.
This flow is expressed by the pressure difference (ΔP) between the peripheral veins (Pvp) and the venous pressure in the right atrium and the venae cavae (central venous pressure Pvc).
Cardiac output is the volume of blood flowing out of the heart to the periphery. Under normal conditions cardiac output and venous return are closely controlled to be equal.

Studying the mechanism of venous circulation amounts to studying the factors which create the pressure gradient between the beginning and the end of the system, that is to say between all the first Venules on the one hand and the right atrium (OD) on the other hand.
Contraction of the left ventricle (LV): sole cause of circulation
At the level of the return circulation, there is a pressure difference, in the subject in a horizontal position:
-the pressure in the Venules is 10 to 15mmHg: the residual energy provided by the contraction of the LV.
-at the junction of the venae cavae in the right atrium, the pressure, “central venous pressure” is close to 0.
It is therefore this gradient, however weak it may be, which constitutes the main and only constant force bringing the blood towards the right atrium.
Contraction of the left ventricle (LV): sole cause of circulation
The suppression of the function of the VG is followed by the almost immediate cessation of all circulation.
Then, venous blood flow which still depends on left ventricular contraction is modulated by different factors.
1-Right ventricular activity (RV): suction power of the RV
RV activity responsible for depression in the OD:
-in diastole, during the rapid filling phase, because part of the blood contained in the DO then passes into the RV;
-in systole, during ejection: the atrioventricular valves are pulled downward, which increases the capacity of the atria.
This has the effect of drawing blood from the large veins into the atria.
This aspiration phenomenon contributes appreciably to venous return.
1-Right ventricular activity (RV): suction power of the RV

During inspiration, contraction of the diaphragm increases abdominal pressure, while intrathoracic pressure decreases. The flow of the cervical veins and upper limbs increases while the blood contained in the inferior vena cava is propelled towards the right atrium.
On the other hand, the release of blood flow from the femoral veins is slowed down due to the increase in abdominal pressure.

When exhaling, on the contrary, the diaphragm relaxes. Intra-abdominal pressure decreases, while intrathoracic pressure increases. The flow of the femoral veins then flows freely towards the vena cava, while the flow of the cervical veins and the upper limbs is slowed down.
In the limbs, the veins are surrounded by skeletal muscles and the contraction of these muscles during activity compresses the veins. Pulsations from nearby arteries could also compress the veins.
Because the venous valves prevent retrograde flow, blood progresses toward the heart.

In a subject standing still, the effect of gravity is maximum and the pressure in the veins of the ankle is approximately 100mmHg. This increase does not constitute an obstacle to the return of blood to the heart, but simply a force tending to distend the venous wall.

During standing, rhythmic contractions of the leg muscles propel the blood towards the heart and can lower the venous pressure of the legs to less than 30mm Hg: at the level of the deep veins, the surrounding tissues maintain a counter pressure which limits the increase in transmural pressure (intravascular pressure - extravascular pressure).
Increased volume of blood returning to the heart

When walking, the operation of the plantar cast (crushing the plantar venous sole) and the venomuscular pump of the calves drives out the blood contained in the veins located under the plant and within the muscle masses and, thanks to the normal play of the valves, helps reduce leg blood pressure while increasing central venous pressure.
In patients with varicose veins (varicose veins), the return of blood to the heart is reduced because their valves are defective. These patients may develop venous stasis and ankle edema.
However, even if the valves are defective, muscle contractions move blood toward the heart because the resistance in the large veins toward the heart is lower than in the small peripheral vessels.
In a standing still position, the gravitational force is responsible for an accumulation of blood in the lower part of the body, by filling and, possibly, dilation of the veins of the lower limbs.

This shift in blood volume leads to a significant reduction in central venous pressure (equivalent to the pressure in the right atrium and the end-diastolic pressure in the right ventricle), and therefore, via the mechanism described by Starling, a reduction in stroke volume.
The reduction in stroke volume is responsible for a transient drop in blood pressure which, in certain patients and under certain conditions, can cause discomfort: orthostatic hypotension.
The baroreflex normally allows this disturbance to be corrected fairly quickly.
Associated venoconstriction makes it possible to mobilize part of the venous reservoir and support central venous pressure.

Blood flows through blood vessels including veins, primarily by the pumping action of the heart. However, venous flow is facilitated by the activity of the right ventricle, by respiratory movements and by the contractions of the skeletal muscles which compress the veins (muscle pump).
